newsitem.title: USA: BT/Telefonica venture sets sights on Brazil/Mexico.
newsitem.headline: BT/Telefonica venture sets sights on Brazil/Mexico.

text.p: Brazil and Mexico head the list of Latin American markets targeted as top priorities in Telefonica's alliance with British Telecom and MCI Communications Corp, executives said.

"The deal will allow us to continue to expand into the two main markets in Latin America -- Brazil and Mexico," said Fernando Panizo, managing director of TISA, the overseas holding company of Spanish national phone company Telefonica.
Under the deal, Telefonica agreed to form a 50/50 Pan American joint venture with BT and MCI managed by TISA.

The Pan-American deal represents the first part of a two- stage strategic alliance, Panizo said. The second stage will focus on Europe, where Telefonica and BT are considering joint investments in various European countries, he said.
Telefonica must first extricate itself from its existing relationships to the AT&T-led Unisource consortium of European phone companies, which competes with the BT-MCI Concert group.

Telefonica already holds significant stakes ranging in size from 22 to 44 percent in leading local, long distance and wireless operators in Argentina, Chile, Columbia and Peru. TISA also owns a 13.5 percent stake in a regional Brazilian telco.
Now as part of its pact with Concert, Telefonica plans to take a one-third stake in Avantel, MCI's long distance venture with finacial services group Banamex in Mexico.
Panizo acknowledged that several previous efforts by Telefonica to gain a foothold in Mexico had failed.

Telefonica, known for its expertise in building local phone services and marketing its products to Spanish-speaking markets, promises to transform Avantel into the leading full-service phone rival to state-owned Telmex.

Brazil is widely seen as the Latin American market with the largest potential for growth, with recent moves to open up long distance, wireless and data services markets and the raging debate over the break-up of local phone monopolies.
Panizo said the new joint venture will be coordinated to take advantage of alliances announced earlier this week that interconnect Portugal Telecom with both BT-MCI and Telefonica.
In Brazil, this network of alliances, anticipates the breakup of Telebras SA, Brazil's national phone holding company, into four or five regional local phone providers.
"With the liberalization of the market and the separation of Telebras...we see an opportunity to bid for those companies we consider relevant to our strategy," Panizo said.
Lending weight to the strategy is Portugal Telecom's existing joint venture with the state-controlled Telebras.

Panizo sees the potential audience of the Pan-American joint venture's services numbering 500 million people, including 300 million Telefonica ventures already serve and the 30 million Spanish speakers living in the United States.
The Pan-American pact builds on MCI's existing links between North and South America.
"There is a huge market for us in both directions," Tim Price, MCI's president and chief operating officer said in a separate interview Friday.
"The deal gives us entry into a $36 billion Latin American market that is expected to grow to $60 billion in the next three years," Price said of market estimates for Year 2000.
"This will give us a seamless network from the Cape to the North Pole," Price boasted.

Price said the first services to result from the joint Pan-American venture would be made available by year-end. He declined to comment on where the joint venture would be headquarted, saying it was under discussion by the partners.
